title: Segment Anything (SAM)
hook: Click a point or drag a box, and it instantly masks the object — even in images it has never seen. SAM is a foundation model for segmentation.
key_points: A promptable segmentation model: give it a point, box, or rough mask and it returns object masks.
Generalizes zero-shot to new images and objects it wasn't explicitly trained on.
Trained on a massive dataset of masks built with a model-assisted labeling loop.
Separates a heavy image encoder from a lightweight prompt-driven mask decoder for fast interaction.
content_html: Alexander Kirillov, Eric Mintun, and colleagues at Meta built SAM as a foundation model for image segmentation. Instead of training one model per dataset, they made it promptable: point at something or draw a box, and SAM outputs a mask for it. Trained on an enormous, model-assisted mask dataset, it segments objects in new images zero-shot.
extra_html:
How it works

SAM has three parts: a heavy image encoder (a ViT) that processes the image once into an embedding, a prompt encoder that ingests points, boxes, or coarse masks, and a lightweight decoder that combines them to produce masks in real time. Because the expensive encoding happens once per image, you can fire off many prompts cheaply and interactively. To get training data at scale, the team ran a data engine where SAM itself proposed masks that annotators corrected, looping until they had a very large, diverse mask dataset.

Why it matters

Segmentation usually means collecting labels and training a fresh model for each new domain. SAM reframes it as a general, promptable capability you can drop into many tasks without retraining, and its released dataset and model became widely used tools. It is a clear example of the foundation-model approach reaching beyond language into pixel-level vision.
